analysis.one_liner: Repeals the core Affordable Care Act coverage rules and lets insurers sell plans nationwide under their home state's rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its House committee referrals and died without a vote when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, despite 51 Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out Title I of the Affordable Care Act — the part that guarantees people can buy coverage regardless of health history, requires plans to cover a standard set of benefits, and helps pay for coverage. It would also let a health insurer pick one state as its 'primary state' and sell individual plans in every other state under that state's rules, skipping the other states' benefit requirements and most of their consumer protections. Insurers would still owe taxes, submit to financial exams, join state guaranty funds, and follow rules on fraud and claims handling.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers gain the ability to shop for the most permissive state regulator and sell cheaper, skinnier plans nationwide. Healthy individual-market buyers would have access to lower-premium plans that skip state-mandated benefits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets an insurer designate one 'primary state' whose laws govern its individual policies everywhere, and exempts it from other states' laws that would prohibit or regulate its operation, though it still must pay state taxes, register locally, submit to financial exams, join insolvency guaranty funds, and follow rules on fraud and unfair claims settlement.
It repeals Title I of the Affordable Care Act and restores the prior law, which supporters argued would bring back cheaper insurance options for people who found ACA-compliant plans unaffordable.

The bill includes some guardrails: insurers may not reclassify a policyholder or raise that individual's premium based on health status at renewal, policies sold across state lines require an independent external appeals process, the primary state must use a risk-based capital formula, and buyers get a bold-print notice that the policy may skip benefits their state requires.

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions would lose guaranteed access to coverage, and low- and middle-income buyers would lose the ACA's subsidies and required benefits. Residents of secondary states would get plans exempt from their own state's mandated benefits, consumer protection laws, and restrictions on rate changes. State insurance regulators would lose most authority over plans sold to their residents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pre-existing-condition patients and ACA subsidy recipients

drawbacks.text: Repealing ACA Title I ends guaranteed issue regardless of health history, the required package of covered benefits, and the premium subsidies that help people afford coverage.

The bill's own required disclosure tells buyers a policy 'may be less expensive than others because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state, including mandated benefits, and 'is not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes' of that state — a built-in acknowledgment that cheaper plans come with fewer protections.

A GAO study is required only after the fact; the bill directs the Comptroller General to study effects on the uninsured, on availability and cost for people with pre-existing conditions, on benefit reductions, and on fraud over the five years after the rules take effect, rather than before.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cheaper plans for healthy buyers are a real benefit, but the bill carries them by stripping the rules that make coverage work for people who are sick or poorer: guaranteed issue, required benefits, subsidies, and home-state consumer protections. Because an insurer could sell nationally under whichever state regulates least, the practical floor for what a plan must cover would be set by the most permissive state, and the bill's own disclosure language concedes buyers give up protections. The repeal component alone would touch millions of coverage arrangements, far outweighing the narrower savings for healthy purchasers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to health subcommittees, never received a markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on January 5, 2017, joined by five original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees on the day of introduction.
In late January 2017 it was referred to the health subcommittees, and the record shows no further action — no subcommittee or full committee vote, no floor debate.
Fifty-one Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, having never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on Affordable Care Act protections — guaranteed coverage regardless of health history, required benefits, and subsidies — kept them, and state governments kept full authority over insurance sold to their residents, because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 supporters — the sponsor and 51 cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the Republican-controlled committees to which it was referred never scheduled action.

industries.note: The bill lets an insurer pick a single 'primary state' and sell individual plans in every other state exempt from those states' benefit mandates and most consumer protection and rate rules, owing only taxes, financial exams, guaranty-fund dues, and fraud and claims-handling standards. That regulatory arbitrage would let insurers sell skinnier plans whose lower cost comes from dropped benefits and protections that ordinary policyholders would otherwise have.
